body.text: Direct supervision is one of three categories of qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) for the U.S. R&D tax credit. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2), it covers only first-line managers who immediately oversee employees performing qualified research; higher-level "two-up" executives are excluded, and claims require contemporaneous, project-level time records.
Executive Summary: Statutory Role and Compliance Risk of Direct Supervision

The classification of supervisory labor as Direct Supervision represents one of the most consequential—and heavily audited—determinations in calculating the United States Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), "qualified services" that generate eligible in-house research wage expenditures are restricted to three statutory categories: engaging in qualified research, engaging in the direct supervision of qualified research, and engaging in the direct support of qualified research. The statutory inclusion of direct supervision recognizes that immediate technical direction, experimental review, and hypothesis refinement are functionally inseparable from the physical or computational execution of a process of experimentation. Because technical leads and engineering managers typically command higher compensation than junior researchers, properly substantiating direct supervision transforms high-value managerial time from non-qualifying overhead into Qualified Research Expenses (QREs), directly expanding the available tax credit and reducing corporate tax liability. Furthermore, when an employee's qualified services reach or exceed the regulatory "substantially all" threshold of 80% of total paid services during the taxable year, 100% of that individual's annual Form W-2 wages qualify as QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(2).

Despite its substantial economic value, Direct Supervision operates under a narrow regulatory definition designed by the Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to prevent general corporate overhead from eroding the statutory tax base. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2) restricts Direct Supervision exclusively to the "immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research". This regulatory gate imposes a strict "one-up" hierarchical boundary: a qualifying supervisor must directly manage the personnel who physically or digitally execute the qualified research activity (QRA). Higher-level managers to whom first-line supervisors report—frequently described as "two-up" or second-tier executives—are categorically excluded from claiming Direct Supervision wages, even when those executives hold advanced scientific credentials or possess deep technical proficiency. Consequently, compliance depends on demonstrating both organizational proximity and contemporaneous, project-level technical nexus, particularly as redesigned IRS Form 6765 reporting rules mandate the disclosure of officers' wages in Section E (effective for 2024 returns) and the explicit disaggregation of wage QREs by business component into direct research, direct supervision, and direct support categories in Section G (optional for 2024 and 2025 returns, and mandatory beginning with 2026 tax year returns).
Legal and Regulatory Architecture of Qualified Services
Tripartite Codification under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)

The statutory authority for including supervisory compensation in the R&D tax credit base derives from IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), which defines "in-house research expenses" to include any wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), the term "wages" carries the meaning assigned by IRC § 3401(a), encompassing taxable remuneration reported on Form W-2—such as base salaries, bonuses, and taxable stock option redemptions—while excluding non-taxed fringe benefits and any wages taken into account in determining the IRC § 51(a) work opportunity credit. IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) establishes the exhaustive three-part definition of qualified services, while Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c) delineates the operational boundaries separating each tier.

The first category, Engaging in Qualified Research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1), encompasses the hands-on, actual conduct of qualified research, illustrated in the regulations by a laboratory scientist personally performing experiments or a software engineer writing and debugging experimental code. The second category, Direct Supervision under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2), captures the immediate, first-line management of those hands-on research activities—exemplified by a research scientist who directly oversees laboratory experiments, evaluates daily test failures, and directs iterative parameter adjustments without personally executing the physical work. The third category, Direct Support under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3), covers ancillary but essential activities that directly support either (i) persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. Regulatory examples of direct support include a clerk compiling experimental data, a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research, a laboratory worker cleaning research equipment, or a machinist machining a component of an experimental model used in qualified research. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3) explicitly stipulates that direct support does not include supervision; supervisory services constitute qualified services only to the extent provided in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2).

cells: Actual hands-on conduct and execution of the process of experimentation.
Scientist conducting laboratory experiments; junior engineer coding and debugging an experimental encryption protocol.
High-level technical consultation or strategic planning divorced from hands-on experimental execution.
Immediate ("first-line" / "one-up") technical management and direction of personnel conducting qualified research.
Research scientist overseeing laboratory experiments; Senior Tech Lead reviewing code commits, setting testing protocols, and directing next-iteration parameters.
Higher-level ("two-up" or above) managers supervising first-line managers; general administrative, budgetary, or commercial strategy oversight.
Services directly supporting personnel who are either engaging in or directly supervising qualified research.
Machinist fabricating an experimental prototype part; clerk compiling research data; secretary typing laboratory result reports; worker cleaning lab equipment.
General and administrative (G&A) services (e.g., payroll, HR, accounting, general janitorial) or services only indirectly beneficial to research activities.

body.text: The Exclusion of General and Administrative Services

A foundational compliance principle governing the credit calculation is that Direct Supervision functions as a strict legal filter against the inclusion of general and administrative (G&A) expenses. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) and (3), neither direct supervision nor direct support includes G&A services or any other activities that provide only an indirect benefit to research operations. Specifically, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3) and IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) instructions confirm that services of payroll personnel preparing salary checks for laboratory scientists, accountants accounting for research expenses, janitors performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, or corporate officers supervising financial or personnel matters do not qualify. Crucially, this exclusion applies based on the functional nature of the activity rather than departmental placement: administrative, human resources, accounting, or budgetary personnel situated entirely inside a dedicated R&D division remain excluded to the extent their duties are administrative rather than directly technical.

Because first-line technical managers routinely split their workdays between qualifying technical direction—such as evaluating experimental data, reviewing code commits, or altering a testing hypothesis—and non-qualifying administrative management—such as conducting annual performance evaluations, approving departmental budgets, or managing staffing schedules—supervisory roles exhibit an inherently mixed activity profile. This functional ambiguity elevates the audit vulnerability of Direct Supervision claims relative to hands-on engineering claims, requiring granular separation between project-specific technical direction and general administrative governance.
Hierarchical Compliance Boundaries: The "One-Up" Rule and Judicial Precedent
Functional Mechanics of the "One-Up" First-Line Management Standard

The primary source of controversy during IRS examinations of supervisory QREs is the rigid enforcement of the "one-up" hierarchical boundary. Both Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guides—including the general Research Credit ATG (Chapter 4, Qualified Research Expenses) and the Pharmaceutical Industry Research Credit Audit Guidelines—establish that Direct Supervision is strictly limited to first-line managers who sit immediately above the researchers executing the experiments. Supervision exercised by a higher-level manager to whom first-line supervisors report does not constitute Direct Supervision, even when that senior manager is a credentialed "qualified research scientist".

Within a typical multi-tier corporate engineering hierarchy, qualification depends entirely on immediate functional proximity to the experimental work rather than executive authority. At the foundational execution tier, junior engineers and bench scientists qualify under "Engaging in Qualified Research" while machinists and data clerks assisting them qualify under "Direct Support". Immediately above those performers sits the first-line management tier, where a Senior Tech Lead or Research Team Lead reviews code commits, evaluates daily test failures, establishes testing protocols, and directs technical parameters for the next experimental iteration; this role satisfies the "one-up" mandate and qualifies as Direct Supervision. By contrast, a peer Product Manager sitting in that same middle tier who focuses on market strategy, customer requirements, and commercial fit is excluded from Direct Supervision unless specifically dictating technical specifications to resolve technological uncertainty. Finally, at the executive tier one level higher, a Vice President of Engineering or Chief Operating Officer (COO) who oversees first-line leads, manages departmental budgets, and allocates capital resources across divisions is a "two-up" manager excluded from Direct Supervision under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2).

The IRS Audit Techniques Guides instruct examiners to evaluate credit eligibility based solely on what an employee actually did (or did not do) during the specific taxable period rather than relying on job titles, generic position descriptions, or an employee's educational and technical qualifications. Formal corporate organizational charts therefore serve as primary examination evidence requested in initial Information Document Requests (IDRs) that can immediately undermine unsubstantiated high-wage supervisory claims. When an organizational chart places a corporate officer or division head two or more tiers above the bench scientists or software engineers, any claim that the executive's managerial oversight qualifies as Direct Supervision is presumptively invalid under Treasury regulations.
Judicial Enforcement and the Moore (Nevco) and Shami Disallowance Principles

Federal courts reviewing R&D tax credit substantiation have strictly enforced the regulatory exclusion of multi-tier management and unsubstantiated executive time allocations. In the landmark decision Scott Moore and Gayla Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20 (Dkt. No. 18632-19, decided February 23, 2023, Judge Colvin), affirmed, Moore v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, No. 23-2681 (7th Cir. Apr. 30, 2024, Circuit Judge Easterbrook), the United States Tax Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit addressed supervisory wage QRE claims made by Nevco, Inc. (Nevco), a Subchapter S corporation that manufactured electronic scoreboards, video displays, and sports-venue equipment. For tax years 2014 and 2015, the taxpayers claimed 65% of the salary and bonuses paid to Nevco's President and Chief Operating Officer (COO), Gary Robert (whose base compensation was $85,092 in 2014 and $178,956 in 2015, plus bonuses), across five product development projects (Scoreboard Truss, Scorbitz, New Caney Ribbon Board, MPCX-2, and Slim Shot Clock), resulting in IRS deficiency determinations of $68,263 for 2014 and $141,945 for 2015.

During examination and trial, the IRS conceded that the wages of Nevco's frontline engineering department employees and their immediate supervisor constituted valid QREs. However, the Tax Court held that Nevco could not include any portion of President/COO Gary Robert's wages in computing its IRC § 41 credit for 2014 or 2015 on two converging structural and evidentiary grounds:

items: Failure of the "One-Up" Direct Supervision and Direct Support Standards: As detailed in the Tax Court record and legal case analyses, Nevco's frontline engineers were directly supervised by its Director of Engineering, Dave Paslay, while President/COO Gary Robert supervised Paslay. Because Robert stood two organizational layers removed from the underlying engineering work ("supervision of supervision") rather than providing first-line management to the researchers performing qualified services, the Tax Court concluded that Robert did not engage in Direct Supervision under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2). Similarly, Robert's executive involvement in budgeting, personnel requirements, and inventory management constituted excluded G&A oversight rather than Direct Support under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3).

Failure to Substantiate Hands-On Qualified Research vs. Broader "New Product Development": Although trial testimony indicated that Robert spent 50% to 65% of his time on "new product development," served as a direct supervisor to a few engineers on specific tasks, and was a named inventor on the Scorbitz patent, the Tax Court held that "new product development" is broader than statutory "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d) because it includes non-qualifying market research, aesthetic design, administrative planning, and customer feedback. Nevco maintained payroll records showing total hours worked, but kept no contemporaneous, task-specific records under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) isolating what fraction of Robert's time was devoted to conducting or directly supervising qualified research. On appeal, the Seventh Circuit affirmed, holding that without records answering both "was it qualified research?" and "how much of Robert's time was devoted to it?", the mathematical credit formula under IRC § 41(a)(1) cannot be calculated, and the Tax Court's factual finding against the taxpayers was free of clear error.

body.text: This precedent reinforces the earlier appellate framework established in Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, aff'd in relevant part, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014), where Farouk Systems, Inc. (FSI) attempted to claim 100% of the multi-million-dollar compensation of its CEO (Farouk Shami) and Co-Chairman (John McCall) for tax years 2003 through 2005 under the 80% "substantially all" rule. In Shami, as documented in case law analyses, the company's laboratory chemists and technicians were directly supervised by an R&D Manager (Ali Ghannad), who reported to CEO Farouk Shami. The Tax Court and the Fifth Circuit rejected the claim, holding that "second-tier supervision"—supervising the R&D Manager who supervises the chemists—does not constitute Direct Supervision under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2), that being named on a patent does not substantiate the hours spent on qualified services, that allocating $8 million to $9.5 million annually in executive salary to R&D without day-to-day technical documentation violates the reasonableness requirement of IRC § 174(e), and that Cohan estimation is unavailable where the taxpayer fails to establish a threshold foundation of qualified services. Conversely, in Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, the Tax Court recognized that while senior executives at Estech Systems, Inc. (ESI) had high-level managerial responsibilities, specific portions of executive time could qualify where corroborated by detailed evidence of direct participation in senior product strategy ideation and systematic beta-testing bug resolution within a documented, multi-level process of experimentation.
Cascading Risk to Direct Support Personnel and Senior Technical Performers

Two critical second-order compliance consequences flow from the "one-up" restriction. First, senior managers face a narrow reclassification path when excluded from Direct Supervision. Although senior research directors, Vice Presidents of Engineering, or Chief Technology Officers cannot qualify under Direct Supervision when managing first-line leads, they may still perform hands-on technical work—such as personally formulating an algorithm or solving a complex engineering bottleneck—that qualifies under the "Engaging in Qualified Research" category. However, as emphasized in the IRS ATGs, such hands-on technical execution typically represents only a "minor fraction" or small fraction of a senior executive's total annual work. Because this minor fraction falls far below the 80% "substantially all" threshold, the IRS Pharmaceutical Industry Research Credit Audit Guidelines instruct examiners to subject any wage claims for employees above first-line supervision to heightened scrutiny of business calendars, travel records, project reports, laboratory books, budget responsibility documents, and live employee interviews to isolate those exact hands-on hours amidst predominantly non-qualifying managerial duties.

Second, improper supervisory claims create a contagion risk for Direct Support personnel. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)(i)–(ii), Direct Support qualifies only to the extent the support employee assists individuals who are either "engaging in actual conduct of qualified research" or "directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research". Consequently, if a taxpayer improperly classifies a "two-up" manager under Direct Supervision and that manager's QRE claim is disallowed upon examination, the disallowance severs the regulatory nexus for any support staff—such as data analysts, administrative clerks, or technical secretaries—who report exclusively to that disallowed manager.
Quantitative Allocation Mechanics and Worked Compliance Scenarios
The 80% "Substantially All" Threshold vs. Prorated Time-Ratio Allocation

The economic impact of Direct Supervision is governed by the mathematical interaction between the "Substantially All" rule of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and the prorated allocation mandate of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2) and IRS ATG calculation rules, "substantially all" of an employee's services consist of qualified services only if 80% or more of the employee's total paid time (or wages allocated on a time-ratio basis, excluding sick leave) during the taxable year is dedicated to qualified services across engaging in research, direct supervision, and direct support combined. Expressing the employee's Qualified Services Ratio across total annual hours worked as a fraction of qualified hours to total hours:
Qualified Services Ratio = Qualified Hours ÷ Total Annual Hours Worked
The employee's eligible Qualified Research Expense wages relative to total annual IRC § 3401(a) Form W-2 wages are governed by the following piecewise function:
Eligible QRE Wages = Total W-2 Wages, if Qualified Services Ratio ≥ 0.80; Total W-2 Wages × Qualified Services Ratio, if Qualified Services Ratio < 0.80

When the Qualified Services Ratio is at least 0.80 (80%), the statute grants a safe-harbor cliff benefit: 100% of the supervisor's annual Form W-2 wages are treated as QREs, absorbing up to 20% of non-qualifying administrative time into the credit base and simplifying compliance defense. Conversely, if the Qualified Services Ratio falls below 0.80—even to 0.79 (79%)—Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) requires strict proration by multiplying total annual wages paid or incurred for the employee by the ratio of total time actually spent performing qualified services to total time spent performing all services for the employer during the taxable year, unless the taxpayer can demonstrate a more appropriate allocation method.
Hypothetical Worked Examples of Supervisory Wage Allocation

To clarify the exact operational application of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c) and (d) across the distinct organizational roles analyzed in this report, the following four hypothetical worked scenarios compute eligible QRE wages step by step.
Hypothetical Example 1: First-Line Research Team Lead Exceeding the 80% Threshold

Assume a software company employs a First-Line Research Team Lead who directly supervises a team of junior software engineers developing a novel encryption protocol to eliminate technical uncertainty regarding methodology reliability. The Team Lead earns $180,000 in annual Form W-2 wages across 2,000 total work hours during the taxable year. Contemporaneous project logs establish that the Team Lead dedicated 1,700 hours to Direct Supervision of the QRA—reviewing daily test failures, selecting alternative coding architectures, setting testing protocols, and directing next-iteration experimental parameters for the junior engineers—while spending the remaining 300 hours on non-qualified general administration such as conducting annual personnel performance reviews and attending general corporate administrative meetings.

To compute the eligible QRE wages, the taxpayer first calculates the Qualified Services Ratio by dividing the 1,700 hours of direct technical supervision by the 2,000 total hours worked, which equals 1,700 / 2,000 = 0.85 (85%). Because the Qualified Services Ratio of 0.85 is greater than or equal to the 0.80 threshold, the Team Lead satisfies the "substantially all" rule under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2). Consequently, 100% of the Team Lead's annual compensation ($180,000 × 100% = $180,000) qualifies as an in-house research expense. By crossing the 80% threshold, the taxpayer lawfully claims the entire $180,000 salary rather than the prorated $153,000 ($180,000 × 0.85), capturing an additional $27,000 in QREs through the statutory safe harbor.
Hypothetical Example 2: Mixed-Duty First-Line Supervisor Below the 80% Threshold

Assume an engineering manager acts as a first-line supervisor over prototype testing engineers, earning $160,000 in annual Form W-2 wages across 2,000 total work hours. Contemporaneous project tracking logs show that the manager spent 900 hours (45%) on Direct Supervision of the QRA (approving technical prototype redesigns and directing laboratory test iterations), 300 hours (15%) personally Engaging in Qualified Research (executing hands-on CAD modeling and stress-testing calculations), and 800 hours (40%) on non-qualified administrative and commercial tasks (managing departmental budgets, HR evaluations, and vendor negotiations).

Aggregating the manager's qualified time across both eligible categories yields 1,200 qualified hours (900 hours + 300 hours). Dividing 1,200 qualified hours by the 2,000 total annual hours produces a Qualified Services Ratio of 0.60 (60%). Because 0.60 is less than 0.80, the "substantially all" rule does not apply, and total qualifying wages must be prorated strictly by the time ratio under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1), yielding $160,000 × 0.60 = $96,000 in eligible QRE wages. The remaining $64,000 ($160,000 × 0.40) is excluded as non-qualifying administrative overhead. Furthermore, to comply with the business-component wage disaggregation requirements on Section G of revised Form 6765, the taxpayer must report $72,000 ($160,000 × 0.45, or 45%) on Line 51 as Direct Supervision wages and $24,000 ($160,000 × 0.15, or 15%) on Line 50 as Direct Research wages, summing to $96,000 in total qualified wages on Line 53.
Hypothetical Example 3: Disallowed "Two-Up" Executive vs. Commercial Product Manager

Assume a Vice President (VP) of Engineering reports to the Chief Technology Officer and supervises four Research Team Leads who in turn supervise the junior engineers. The VP earns $250,000 in annual Form W-2 wages across 2,000 total work hours, spending 1,200 hours (60%) supervising the first-line Research Team Leads ("two-up" oversight), 600 hours (30%) reviewing quarterly R&D budgets and approving capital expenditures, and 200 hours (10%) personally writing and testing a specialized encryption sub-routine.

Applying the "one-up" exclusion under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) and the Moore v. Commissioner / Shami v. Commissioner holdings, because the VP is two organizational tiers removed from the engineers conducting the research, 0 hours of the 1,200 supervisory hours qualify as Direct Supervision, and 0 hours of the 600 budgetary hours qualify. Only the 200 hours of personal hands-on coding qualify under the "Engaging in Qualified Research" category, yielding a Qualified Services Ratio of 200 / 2,000 = 0.10 (10%) and eligible QRE wages of $250,000 × 0.10 = $25,000. Thus, $225,000 (90%) of the VP's salary is non-qualifying overhead. Similarly, a peer Commercial Product Manager earning $150,000 across 2,000 hours whose oversight focuses entirely on market strategy and customer requirements rather than resolving technical uncertainty through first-line experimental direction logs 0 qualified hours (0%) and generates $0 in Direct Supervision QREs.
Audit Defense, Substantiation Standards, and Emerging Reporting Mandates
IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) Scrutiny and Oral Interview Protocols

IRS Audit Techniques Guides explicitly instruct examiners to target supervisory wage claims that appear to extend beyond first-line management or rely on generalized percentage estimates. Under Chapter 4 (Qualified Research Expenses) and Chapter 7 (Substantiation and Recordkeeping) of the IRS Research Credit ATG, the auditor's core inquiry is two-fold: determining what the supervisor actually did and verifying how much time was spent doing it. At the outset of an examination, examiners issue focused Information Document Requests (IDRs) seeking organizational charts, employee Form W-2s, payroll registers, job descriptions, annual performance evaluations, business calendars, appointment books, travel records, project reports, and laboratory notebooks.

Because formal titles and generic job descriptions are treated as unreliable indicators of actual functional duties, IRS examiners routinely conduct live oral interviews with claimed supervisors to test the internal consistency of the taxpayer's written documentation. Chapter 7 of the IRS ATG recommends that interviews of technical and supervisory personnel be conducted by a two-person IRS team—the primary examiner paired with a second IRS colleague who acts as an observer, takes detailed notes, and poses follow-up questions—to evaluate, confirm, clarify, or refute documentary claims. If a supervisor's oral testimony describes their day-to-day role in terms of high-level strategy, resource allocation, or departmental administration—contradicting time logs or consultant studies that claim 85% hands-on technical supervision—the examiner has grounds to reject the taxpayer's allocation method, disallow the supervisory wage claim in full, and, where recordkeeping is systemically deficient, issue a formal Notice of Inadequate Records (Letter 978 (DO), Letter 979 (DO), or Letter 1022 (DO)) pursuant to IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(d). Conversely, Large Business and International (LB&I / formerly LMSB) taxpayers may proactively mitigate substantiation disputes for prospective tax years by entering into a Research Credit Recordkeeping Agreement (RCRA) under IRS Notice 2004-11.
The Business Component Nexus Imperative and Contemporaneous Recordkeeping

Under IRC § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC § 41 must retain records in "sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit". As detailed in IRS Field Attorney Advice (FAA) Memorandum 20212501F and judicial rulings including Moore v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-20, aff'd, 7th Cir. 2024) and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, establishing this "nexus" requires connecting each supervisor's claimed time directly to a qualifying "business component" (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business) that separately satisfies the four-part statutory test of IRC § 41(d)(1)–(3):

items: Section 174 / Section 174A Eligibility Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)): Expenditures must qualify as research or experimental expenditures in the experimental or laboratory sense under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) (and, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A).

Discovering Technological Information Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)): The research must be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature, fundamentally relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4).

Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) & § 41(d)(3)(A)): The application of that information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component for a qualified purpose relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)).

Process of Experimentation Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)): Substantially all (80% or more under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)) of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)—identifying technical uncertainty, identifying alternatives, and evaluating those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error.

body.text: Traditional cost-center accounting—which aggregates all engineering or R&D department salaries into a single departmental overhead pool—fails to establish business-component nexus. Furthermore, IRS FAA 20212501F confirms that the requirement to substantiate the four-part test and nexus separately for each business component is not waived even when a taxpayer or the IRS utilizes statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42. Taxpayers must therefore deploy project-based accounting systems paired with contemporaneous technical artifacts created in the ordinary course of research, rather than post-hoc reconstructions or year-end questionnaires.

headers: Required Granular Content for Direct Supervision

cells: Substantiating the exact time-ratio allocation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) or the 80% threshold under § 1.41-2(d)(2).
Hours logged contemporaneously by specific business component (project) and segregated by service category (Direct Supervision vs. Hands-On vs. G&A).
Project-based timecards, Jira/sprint tracking logs, payroll registers, and employee Forms W-2.
Proving compliance with the "one-up" first-line management boundary under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2).
Clear mapping demonstrating that the supervisor's immediate direct reports are the engineers or scientists personally executing the QRA.
Dated R&D organizational charts, functional role matrices, performance evaluations, and project team rosters.
Corroborating the technical nexus between the supervisor's oversight and the process of experimentation.
Evidence that the supervisor reviewed experimental data, altered hypotheses, set testing protocols, or directed technical redesigns.
Pull-request/code review logs, testing protocol emails, project progress reports, lab notebooks, design authorizations, and technical meeting minutes.
Verifying functional reality against written time logs and organizational charts during IRS ATG interviews.
Consistent first-hand explanation of daily interactions with junior researchers, specific test plan reviews, and technical uncertainty resolution.
Pre-audit manager interview transcripts, business calendars, and contemporaneous project summaries.

body.text: Form 6765 Wage Disaggregation and IRC Section 174 / Section 174A Interplay
Two major federal tax developments fundamentally alter the compliance and audit-selection profile of Direct Supervision claims.
Redesigned IRS Form 6765 (Sections E, F, and G) and Explicit Wage Disaggregation

Following an 18-month stakeholder feedback process that began with IR-2023-173 in September 2023, the IRS released the finalized four-page redesign of Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Rev. December 2024) on February 11, 2025, followed by updated final Instructions for Form 6765 in February 2026. The redesigned form introduces three new disclosure sections that directly target supervisory and executive wage claims:

items: Section E (Other Information — Lines 37–41): Mandatory starting with the 2024 tax year for all filers reporting QREs, Section E requires taxpayers to report the total number of business components generating QREs (Line 37) and to explicitly disclose on Line 38 the exact dollar amount of officers' wages (determined under the laws of the state of incorporation) included in total qualified wages on Line 42.

Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary — Lines 42–48): Summarizes total qualified wages across all business components on Line 42, total supply costs on Line 43, total computer rental/lease costs on Line 44, and total applicable contract research expenses on Lines 45–47, summing to total QREs on Line 48.

Section G (Business Component Information — Lines 49(a)–49(f) and Lines 50–56): Under official IRS instructions, completing Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (the 2024 and 2025 tax years) and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (starting with the 2026 tax year) on original returns. (Section G exemptions apply on original returns only to Qualified Small Businesses electing the payroll tax credit under IRC § 41(h)(3), or to eligible small businesses with ≤$1.5 million in total QREs and ≤$50 million in average annual gross receipts over the prior three tax years at the controlled-group level; filers submitting amended returns must provide business component details regardless of size). For the "80%/Top 50" business components—components comprising at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 components, plus an "Aggregate Business Components" line in Column 49(c) for any remaining <20% QREs—Page 4 of Form 6765 requires taxpayers to disaggregate qualified wages for each individual business component across four dedicated wage columns: Line 50 (Direct research wages for qualified services), Line 51 (Direct supervision wages for qualified services), Line 52 (Direct support wages for qualified services), and Line 53 (Total qualified wages, summing Lines 50, 51, and 52).

body.text: By requiring taxpayers to disclose officers' wages on Line 38 and to report the exact dollar split among direct research (Line 50), direct supervision (Line 51), and direct support (Line 52) for every major business component, Form 6765 makes top-heavy supervisory claims or unsubstantiated percentage allocations immediately visible to IRS risk-scoring algorithms upon filing.
Interplay Between IRC Section 41, TCJA Section 174 (2022–2024), and OBBBA Section 174A (2025 and Beyond)

Taxpayers must also navigate the complex statutory interplay between the IRC § 41 research credit and the federal income tax treatment of underlying research and experimental (R&E) deductions across two distinct statutory regimes. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) amendments to IRC § 174 and administrative guidance in IRS Notice 2023-63 (as modified by Notice 2024-12) required taxpayers to capitalize "specified research or experimental expenditures" and amortize them over a 5-year period for domestic research and a 15-year period for foreign research using a midpoint convention. Because the definition of R&E expenditures under IRC § 174 is broader than the definition of QREs eligible for the IRC § 41 tax credit, an asymmetric audit risk arises for open 2022–2024 tax years (as well as for ongoing foreign research teams and taxpayers in states that decouple from federal expensing): if an IRS examiner disallows a manager's wages under IRC § 41 because the manager failed the strict "one-up" Direct Supervision test or lacked project-level time logs, those disallowed wages may still remain classified as specified R&E expenditures subject to mandatory capitalization under IRC § 174. In that scenario, the taxpayer loses the immediate dollar-for-dollar IRC § 41 tax credit while still suffering the adverse cash-flow impact of multi-year amortization rather than immediate IRC § 162 deductibility.

On July 4, 2025, the enactment of Public Law 119-21 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act or OBBBA) added IRC § 174A and amended IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Under IRC § 174A (implemented through Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and Rev. Proc. 2026-32), taxpayers may once again immediately deduct domestic R&E expenditures in the year paid or incurred (or elect under IRC § 174A(c) to capitalize and amortize them over at least 60 months beginning when benefits are first realized, while recovering unamortized 2022–2024 domestic balances in 2025 or ratably across 2025 and 2026). However, foreign R&E expenditures remain governed by IRC § 174 and must continue to be capitalized and amortized over 15 years. Furthermore, amended IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) explicitly requires that qualified research for the IRC § 41 credit be research with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A. As Rev. Proc. 2026-32 underscores, IRC § 174A and IRC § 41 apply distinct technical standards: a supervisory wage expenditure that is deductible as domestic R&E under IRC § 174A does not automatically qualify as a Direct Supervision QRE under IRC § 41, and any disallowance or adjustment of Direct Supervision QREs directly alters the mandatory IRC § 280C(c) deduction reduction (unless the reduced credit election under IRC § 280C(c)(2) was timely made on Item A of Form 6765).
Strategic Compliance Recommendations
To mitigate examination exposure and preserve legitimate supervisory QREs under IRC § 41, organizations claiming the R&D tax credit should implement five integrated operational controls:

items: Institute Annual "One-Up" Organizational Chart Audits and Officer Wage Reviews Prior to Year-End Close: Because the organizational chart operates as a primary audit document requested in initial IRS IDRs—and because Form 6765 Section E, Line 38 explicitly flags officers' wages—internal tax teams must review reporting hierarchies against Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) before filing. Internal classification under the "Direct Supervision" category must be restricted exclusively to verified first-line managers whose immediate direct reports perform hands-on qualified research. For senior directors, VPs, and C-suite executives located two or more tiers above the researchers (such as the President/COO in Moore v. Commissioner or the CEO in Shami v. Commissioner), internal policy should prohibit any claim under Direct Supervision and restrict their eligible time logs strictly to documented, hands-on "Engaging in Qualified Research" tasks.

Transition from Cost-Center Accounting to Project-Based Time Tracking Segregated by Service Type: Capturing labor at the specific business-component level establishes the required nexus between supervisory wages and qualified research activities under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) and IRS FAA 20212501F. Time-entry and project-management systems (such as Jira or enterprise timesheets) should be configured to segregate hours across the exact three statutory categories required by Form 6765 Section G—Direct Research (Line 50), Direct Supervision (Line 51), and Direct Support (Line 52)—while maintaining a distinct code for non-qualifying G&A management.

Establish Active Monitoring of the 80% "Substantially All" Threshold for Key Technical Leads: By structuring job responsibilities so that first-line research leads dedicate 80% or more of their annual paid time (excluding sick leave) to Direct Supervision and hands-on research—while offloading routine administrative, HR, and budgetary tasks to dedicated G&A personnel—taxpayers can lawfully secure 100% wage inclusion under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2) and avoid the heightened audit friction associated with defending prorated claims below 80%.

Enforce Contemporaneous Technical Artifact Archiving Paired with Pre-Filing Manager Interviews: First-line supervisors should preserve contemporaneous digital evidence of their technical direction—including pull-request and code review logs, experimental protocol sign-offs, hypothesis revision emails, laboratory notebooks, and technical design review minutes—linked directly to each business component's unique identifier on Form 6765 Column 49(c). Conducting structured internal interviews and mock audit sessions with first-line supervisors during the annual credit study process ("Did you review the test plan?", "Did you alter the experimental hypothesis?") ensures that oral testimony aligns seamlessly with written time logs and organizational charts when examined by a two-person IRS interview team.

Maintain a Unified IRC Section 41, Section 174, and Section 174A Compliance Mapping: Tax departments must coordinate their annual R&D credit studies with their R&E tax accounting method schedules under Rev. Proc. 2025-28 and Rev. Proc. 2026-32. Specifically, taxpayers must reconcile Direct Supervision QREs under IRC § 41 against domestic R&E deductions or elective 60-month capitalization schedules under IRC § 174A (for 2025 and subsequent years), unamortized domestic TCJA IRC § 174 balances (from 2022–2024), foreign 15-year IRC § 174 capitalization schedules, and IRC § 280C(c) reduction computations to prevent unexpected cash-flow shortfalls or accounting method discrepancies upon audit.
